issues.legal_issue: The payment of rent through separate cheques, including a cheque issued in the name of another entity, does not establish a separate tenancy when the original letting was to one tenant and the landlord expressly denied that entity was a tenant.
material_facts: The premises were initially let to one individual under an oral agreement for a single monthly rent.
The tenant later paid the rent in two parts, one by a cheque drawn by himself and the other by a cheque issued in the name of a trust of which he was secretary.
The landlord acknowledged cheques associated with the trust but wrote that he did not recognize the trust as his tenant; those letters went unanswered.
The Rent Controller found that there was one tenancy, while the High Court found that there were two.
issues.conclusion: There was one tenancy between the landlord and the individual tenant; the trust was not a tenant of any part of the premises.
issues.legal_principle: The use of more than one cheque, or a cheque drawn by a third party, does not by itself establish a separate tenancy when the tenant remains liable for the single agreed rent. The Court relied on Sheodhari Rai v. Suraj Prasad Singh, AIR 1954 SC 758, for the proposition that payment arrangements alone do not establish a separate tenancy.

rule.if: rent_control_eviction_proceeding and original_letting_was_to_one_tenant and rent_was_paid_in_parts and landlord_denied_entity_tenancy

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding: A landlord brought a proceeding seeking possession of rented premises under rent-control law.
predicates.original_letting_was_to_one_tenant: The landlord initially agreed to let the premises to one tenant for a single rent.
predicates.rent_was_paid_in_parts: The tenant later paid the agreed rent in separate amounts, including an amount paid by or through another entity.
predicates.landlord_denied_entity_tenancy: The landlord expressly told the tenant that the other entity was not recognized as a tenant.

issues.definition: When a rent-control eviction proceeding involves an original letting to one tenant, divided rent payments, and an express denial that the paying entity is a tenant, the rule treats the arrangement as a single tenancy.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional court under rent-control law may not reassess the merits of factual controversies and reverse a factual finding supported by the material and circumstances.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found, on the evidence and surrounding circumstances, that there was a single tenancy.
The High Court heard a revision under the rent-control law and reversed that factual finding.
The Supreme Court considered the High Court's revisional authority alongside the revision power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should not have interfered with the Rent Controller's finding that there was a single tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: Although section 25B(8) of the Delhi Rent Control Act gives the High Court somewhat wider revisional powers than section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, those powers do not authorize it to enter into the merits of factual controversies and reverse findings of fact. The Court relied on Helper Girdharbhai v. Saiyed Mohmad, [1987] 3 SCC 538, and stated that Sushila Devi v. Avinash Chandra Jain, [1987] 2 SCC 219, established no different principle.

predicates.rent_control_revision_proceeding: A court considered a revision from a rent-control decision.
predicates.finding_was_factual_and_material_based: The original decision-maker reached a factual finding based on the evidence and circumstances before it.

issues.definition: In a rent-control revision, when the challenged finding is factual and based on the material, the revisional court must not reverse that finding by reassessing its merits.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord's bona fide residential requirement is not defeated merely because a professional intends to use part of the residence as an office, library, or study.
material_facts: The landlord was an advocate seeking possession for bona fide residential use by himself and his family, as well as accommodation for his servants.
He intended to use the ground-floor hall as an office and library, partly because ill health made his existing office location unsuitable.
The Rent Controller accepted that the hall's intended professional use fell within the residential-requirement ground; the High Court refused possession of the hall on that basis.
issues.conclusion: The intended use of part of the residence as an office and library did not defeat the landlord's residential requirement, and the High Court should not have denied possession of the hall on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Under clause (e) of the proviso to section 14(1) of the Delhi Rent Control Act, a professional's use of part of a residence as an office, library, or study may be incidental to residential use and does not by itself make the requirement non-residential. The Court relied on Khanna v. Batra, [1966] 2 DLT 306. It distinguished Mohanlal v. Kondi, [1979] 3 SCR 12, and Subramania Mudaliar v. Kolapur Traders, [1981] 4 SCC 511, which concerned a different statutory provision and did not resolve this issue. The Court noted that a claim to premises needed solely as an office and library may not satisfy the residential-requirement provision.

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: A landlord seeks possession of premises on the ground that they are needed for residential use.
predicates.landlord_seeks_bona_fide_home_use: The landlord seeks the premises for a genuine residential need of the landlord or the landlord's family.
predicates.professional_use_confined_to_part: A professional landlord intends to use only part of the premises as an office, library, or study while seeking the premises for residential use.

issues.definition: When a landlord genuinely seeks premises for residential use and confines professional use to part of them, that professional use does not defeat the residential need.
